JEFFREY ABT — “THE ORIGINS OF THE PUBLIC MUSEUM” (2006)
A Companion to Museum Studies, pp. 115–134


1. WHO IS THE AUTHOR?
Jeffrey Abt is an American artist, museum historian and Professor Emeritus at Wayne State University. His career is unusually useful for this reading because it combines studio practice, curatorial work, museum administration and institutional history. He worked at the Wichita Art Museum and at the University of Chicago’s Smart Museum before teaching art, art history and museum studies. His research repeatedly asks how museums produce cultural authority, preserve memory and translate private collecting into public institutions.


DISCIPLINARY CONTEXT
Museum studies + art history + institutional history + cultural history.
Important: Abt is not writing a simple chronology of “the first museums”. He is writing a genealogy of the public museum: how the meanings of “public” and “museum” developed separately and gradually became intertwined.


2. CLEAR SUMMARY OF THE ARTICLE


MAIN THESIS
The public museum does not suddenly appear in 1683 with the Ashmolean or in 1793 with the Louvre. Those are important moments, but Abt traces a much longer history of relations between objects, display, learning, civic authority and audiences.


A. CLASSICAL ANTIQUITY — RES PUBLICA
Abt goes back to Greece and Rome because collecting, scholarly study and civic display already existed there.
• Greek mouseion originally referred to a place associated with the Muses and learning.
• Aristotle’s collecting and classification of natural specimens links collections with empirical study.
• In Hellenistic and Roman contexts, objects move from religious settings into political and civic uses.
• Roman conquest brings Greek art into public urban space as trophies and cultural capital.


CONCEPT — res publica
Latin: “public matter / public affair”.
Why it matters: some objects become connected to civic authority rather than remaining purely private possessions.
Intellectual point: the “public” dimension of museums has roots in political ideas about common civic space, not only in opening hours or ticket policy.


B. RENAISSANCE — PRIVATE COLLECTIONS BECOME CIVIC
Renaissance collections are largely aristocratic, princely and ecclesiastical: studioli, cabinets of curiosities, galleries.
But gradually private collecting acquires civic significance.
Historical example: Medici collections and the Uffizi.
The crucial transition is not simply private → public; it is dynastic possession → civic/national patrimony.
A collection starts representing not only the owner’s taste but also the identity and prestige of a city or polity.


CONCEPT — civic space
A space where political community represents itself through architecture, objects, memory and spectacle.


C. ENLIGHTENMENT — KNOWLEDGE + ACCESS
Enlightenment culture intensifies classification, taxonomy and ideals of rational public education.
Museum = instrument for organising and disseminating knowledge.
Historical example: Ashmolean Museum, founded 1683.
It stipulated public access, but visitors were regulated, guided and charged. “Public” did not mean completely open or socially equal.
Historical example: British Museum, founded 1753 and opened 1759.
Hans Sloane’s private collection becomes a national institution through parliamentary action.
Important transition: private property → national trust.
But public ownership does not automatically mean public authority over interpretation.


Abt’s important point: as museum access widened, the museum in England became not just a building but a social institution accommodating visitors from different backgrounds and classes.


D. THE LOUVRE + REVOLUTION
The Louvre opens as a public museum in 1793 during the French Revolution.
This is politically different from merely allowing visitors into a royal collection.
Royal property is redefined as national patrimony.
The same objects now speak in the name of “the people” rather than the monarch.


CONCEPT — sovereignty
The ultimate political authority in a society.
Museum relevance: when a royal collection becomes national heritage, the political subject represented by the collection changes.


Strong formulation:
The transition from royal collection to public museum is not merely spatial; it is a transfer and redefinition of sovereignty.


But access and authority remain different questions:
Who may enter?
Who owns the objects?
Who classifies them?
Who decides what they mean?


E. NAPOLEON + THE UNIVERSAL MUSEUM
French revolutionary and Napoleonic expansion exported the Louvre model across Europe.
Art confiscated from churches, aristocrats and conquered territories was centralised in museums.
This creates a contradiction:
museum as universal knowledge + museum as product of military and political power.


Question for discussion:
Can an institution claim to preserve “universal” culture when the routes through which objects arrived were highly unequal?


F. NINETEENTH-CENTURY AMERICA — PRIVATISING THE PUBLIC
Abt then shows that the American path differs sharply from European state museums.
Many US museums were founded and governed by private citizens, philanthropists and trustees rather than the state.
Examples: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Museum of Fine Arts Boston.
Private wealth is converted into institutions claiming public purposes.


CONCEPT — public/private hybridity
Ownership, governance, funding, access and mission do not necessarily align.
A museum can be privately governed while claiming a public educational mission.


This is why “public museum” cannot be defined by ownership alone.


G. THE MUSEUM PRODUCES ITS PUBLIC
By the nineteenth century, the question increasingly shifts from “who is admitted?” to “what kind of citizen should the museum help create?”
Museums position themselves around education, public service, morality and social stability.
Museum therefore does not merely receive an existing public; it helps form one.


CONCEPT — subject formation
Institutions help produce norms of behaviour and identity.
Museum example: visitors learn how to behave, what to value, how to classify culture and what counts as legitimate knowledge.


Connection to Tony Bennett:
museum as part of the “exhibitionary complex” — power works through visibility, ordering and self-discipline, not only through prohibition.


H. ABT’S CONCLUSION
Abt rejects a teleological history:
private cabinet → public museum → democracy.
The public museum is a changing institutional form produced by different political, social and economic conditions.
Professionalisation in the late nineteenth century creates a more standardised ideal of what a “public museum” should be, but that ideal continues to evolve.


THE MOST IMPORTANT ANALYTICAL POINT
Publicness is not a single property. Separate:
• ownership
• governance
• funding
• access
• authority
• representation
• accountability


A museum can be “public” in one sense and highly private or exclusionary in another.


3. PARAGRAPHS / PASSAGES FOR DISCUSSION


PASSAGE 1 — p. 127
Key phrase: “social as well as physical space”
Why it matters:
Abt describes the moment when widening museum access changes the institution itself. The museum is no longer only a building containing collections; it becomes a social space in which different classes encounter knowledge.
Discussion:
Does admitting a wider audience democratise the museum if interpretation and classification remain controlled by experts and elites?


PASSAGE 2 — p. 132, conclusion
Key phrase: “steadily evolving institutional form”
Why it matters:
This destroys the idea that the public museum has one stable definition. “Public” must be continuously renegotiated as expectations around access, education, representation and accountability change.
Discussion:
What would make a museum meaningfully public today: free admission, democratic governance, restitution, community authorship, public funding, or something else?


PRESENTATION — SHORT SPEAKING STRUCTURE


AUTHOR
Jeffrey Abt is a museum historian, artist and former museum practitioner whose scholarship focuses on museums as cultural and institutional systems rather than neutral containers.


ARGUMENT
Abt challenges the conventional origin story in which the public museum simply emerges with the Ashmolean or Louvre. He traces a much longer genealogy of “public” and “museum”, from classical civic display through Renaissance collections, Enlightenment access, revolutionary nationalisation and nineteenth-century philanthropy.


KEY POINT
The article separates public access from public authority. A museum may become accessible to wider audiences while authority over collecting, classification and interpretation remains concentrated.


DISCUSSION POINT
The Louvre makes the contradiction especially visible: revolutionary nationalisation converts royal collections into “the people’s” patrimony, but someone still determines the categories through which that heritage is understood.


ONE-SENTENCE THESIS
The history of the public museum is not simply a history of opening doors; it is a history of changing relations between property, knowledge, sovereignty and audiences.


VISUAL QUOTE CARDS
Four slide cards follow below. The quoted fragments are deliberately short; use them as anchors while you explain the surrounding paragraph orally.

JEFFREY ABT — “THE ORIGINS OF THE PUBLIC MUSEUM” (2006)
A Companion to Museum Studies, pp. 115–134


WHO IS THE AUTHOR?
Jeffrey Abt is a scholar and writer on museum history, visual culture, collecting, and the institutional history of museums. His disciplinary position sits between museum studies, art history, and the history of institutions. In this chapter he is less interested in individual artworks than in the historical formation of the museum as a public institution.


Core intellectual move:
Abt does not treat “the public museum” as an obvious or timeless category. He asks how “public” and “museum” came to be linked historically, and what kinds of ownership, access, authority and civic purpose made that possible.


MAIN ARGUMENT
The public museum did not appear suddenly in the eighteenth century as a finished democratic institution. It developed through a long genealogy: classical civic display, Renaissance collecting, Enlightenment ideas of public knowledge, revolutionary nationalisation, and nineteenth-century philanthropic institutions.


The crucial point is that “public” can mean different things:
• public ownership
• public access
• public funding
• public mission
• civic representation
• accountability to a wider community


These are not the same thing.


1. ANTIQUITY: OBJECTS IN THE CIVIC REALM
Abt goes back to classical antiquity because the roots of the public museum lie partly in the idea that certain objects belong to the civic realm rather than exclusively to private owners.


PONЯТИЕ — res publica
Origin: Latin political thought.
Meaning: literally “public matter” or “public affair”; the common civic realm.
Why it matters: Abt uses this genealogy to show that “publicness” existed before the modern museum, but in historically specific forms.


Historical example:
Greek temples and Roman forums displayed cult objects, trophies, sculpture and spoils in spaces of collective civic significance. This was public visibility, but not modern democratic access. Citizenship itself was restricted.


Intellectual takeaway:
“Public” is always historically constructed. It never means exactly the same thing across periods.


2. RENAISSANCE: PRIVATE COLLECTIONS ACQUIRE CIVIC MEANING
Renaissance collecting is largely dynastic, aristocratic and ecclesiastical. Cabinets, studioli and princely galleries stage knowledge and prestige.


Historical example:
The Medici collections and the Uffizi. These collections initially expressed dynastic power, but gradually became understood as part of Florence’s civic and cultural identity.


Key transition:
private/dynastic possession → civic patrimony


PONЯТИЕ — civic patrimony
Meaning: cultural property understood as belonging symbolically to a city or political community rather than only to an individual owner.


Intellectual takeaway:
The museum begins to emerge when collections are no longer only signs of private prestige, but become resources through which a community imagines itself.


3. ENLIGHTENMENT: KNOWLEDGE, CLASSIFICATION, PUBLIC EDUCATION
In the Enlightenment, museums become institutions for ordering and disseminating knowledge.
Objects are collected, catalogued and classified according to type, material, chronology, geography or function.


PONЯТИЕ — epistemic institution
Origin: epistemology = theory of knowledge.
Meaning here: an institution that helps determine how knowledge is organised, validated and made visible.


Strong formula:
The museum does not simply store knowledge; it produces knowledge by organising objects into categories.


Historical example:
The British Museum, founded in 1753 and opened in 1759, grew from the collection of Sir Hans Sloane and became a national institution through an Act of Parliament.


Important contradiction:
A private collection becomes “public”, but this does not mean that the public controls its classification, interpretation or institutional authority.


Strong seminar line:
“Public access does not necessarily mean public authorship of knowledge.”


4. THE LOUVRE: SOVEREIGNTY CHANGES
The Louvre after the French Revolution is crucial because it shows how a museum can re-signify political ownership.


Before:
royal collection


After 1793:
national collection


The artworks often remain materially the same; what changes is the political subject in whose name they are displayed.


PONЯТИЕ — sovereignty
Origin: political theory.
Meaning: ultimate political authority.
Why it matters here: the shift from monarchy to nation changes the meaning of cultural ownership.


Strong formula:
“The transition from royal collection to public museum is not merely spatial; it is a transfer and redefinition of sovereignty.”


5. PUBLIC MUSEUM AS A MACHINE FOR LEGITIMACY
Museums transform possession into representation.


A ruler’s collection represents the ruler.
A national museum claims to represent the nation.
A “universal” museum claims to represent humanity.


This means museums convert ownership into symbolic authority.


Strong formula:
“The museum does not only preserve objects; it redistributes the symbolic authority attached to them.”


6. CLASSIFICATION IS POWER
Enlightenment museums do not simply open knowledge; they classify it.


Classification appears rational and neutral, but it creates hierarchies:
• fine art / craft
• civilisation / primitive
• art / ethnography
• masterpiece / specimen


PONЯТИЕ — classification
Origin: natural history, Enlightenment taxonomy, archaeology, art history.
Why it matters: to classify is to decide what kinds of difference matter.


Theoretical extension:
This can be connected to Michel Foucault: systems of knowledge are never purely descriptive; they organise what can be seen, compared and legitimised.


Strong line:
“Classification is never merely descriptive. It creates hierarchies.”


7. PUBLICNESS DOES NOT EQUAL DEMOCRACY
One of the most useful insights in Abt:
a museum can be public without being democratically controlled.


A museum may be:
• open to all
• publicly funded
• nationally owned
but still be governed by specialists, trustees or elites who control interpretation.


Strong formula:
“The public museum democratizes access without necessarily democratizing authority.”


8. NINETEENTH-CENTURY AMERICA: PRIVATE GOVERNANCE, PUBLIC MISSION
Abt shows that the American museum complicates the simple public/private divide.


Historical example:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, founded in 1870.
Its mission is public, but its governance and philanthropy are private.


PONЯТИЕ — public/private hybridity
Meaning: an institution can combine public mission, private governance, philanthropy, civic education and broad access.


Important consequence:
“Public” is not a single legal category. It can describe mission, audience, funding, ownership or representation.


9. PHILANTHROPY AND CULTURAL POWER
Private wealth can be transformed into public culture.


This appears generous — and often is — but it can also reproduce elite authority.


PONЯТИЕ — cultural capital
Origin: Pierre Bourdieu.
Meaning: prestige, education, taste and symbolic authority that help structure social distinction.


Historical logic:
wealthy patrons donate collections → institutions become public cultural authorities → elite tastes can become canonical standards.


Strong line:
“Private wealth can become public culture without ceasing to reproduce elite authority.”


10. MUSEUMS PRODUCE A PUBLIC
Abt’s history suggests that museums do not merely receive an already existing public.
They help create one.


The museum trains visitors:
• how to look
• how to behave
• what to value
• what counts as history
• what counts as civilisation


This can be connected to Tony Bennett’s idea of the exhibitionary complex.


PONЯТИЕ — exhibitionary complex
Origin: Tony Bennett, influenced by Foucault.
Meaning: museums and exhibitions discipline citizens through visibility, ordering, display and self-regulation rather than only through force.


Strong formula:
“The museum’s public is always double — it is both addressed and produced.”


11. UNIVERSAL MUSEUM: A CONTRADICTION
Museums such as the British Museum or Louvre can claim to represent universal human culture.


But universal collections were often built through:
• empire
• conquest
• unequal exchange
• colonial networks
• diplomatic and military power


This creates a central contradiction:
universal claim vs particular history of acquisition


Strong question:
“Who can legitimately claim to hold objects ‘for humanity’?”


This is directly relevant to current restitution debates.


12. MUSEUM AS MEMORY INFRASTRUCTURE
Museums do not simply preserve all pasts equally.
They select.


What enters a permanent collection, catalogue or display gains institutional legitimacy.
What remains outside may become culturally less visible.


Connection to Massey:
Massey: places have multiple pasts.
Abt: museums are institutions that can make one past canonical.


PONЯТИЕ — canonical memory
Meaning: a version of the past that becomes institutionally authorised and repeatedly reproduced.


13. CONNECTION TO MARTIN BECK
Abt explains how the museum becomes a public institution.
Beck explains how display produces meaning inside that institution.


Abt = institutional authority.
Beck = spatial and visual organisation of meaning.


Strong synthesis:
“Institution determines authority; display determines legibility.”


14. CONNECTION TO HARVEY
Harvey asks:
Who controls urban resources?


Abt asks:
Who controls cultural resources?


In both cases:
formal publicness does not guarantee public control.


15. CONNECTION TO MASSEY
Massey:
who defines place and which pasts become visible?


Abt:
who defines heritage and which histories become public?


Both reveal that “the public” is not neutral; it is constructed through inclusion, exclusion and selective memory.


MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAYS
• The public museum is historically produced, not timeless.
• Public access is not the same as public authority.
• Museums transform private possession into civic, national or universal representation.
• Classification produces knowledge and hierarchy.
• Museums help construct the public they claim to serve.
• The history of the public museum is not a simple story of democratic progress.
• Universal museums often depend on particular imperial and elite histories.


SEMINAR FORMULATIONS
“Abt complicates the idea of the public museum by separating access from authority.”
“The history of the museum is not simply a history of opening doors, but of redefining who may legitimately own, classify and represent culture.”
“What changes from princely collection to public museum is not only ownership, but the political subject in whose name the collection speaks.”
“The public museum is not a finished democratic form but a historically evolving institutional compromise.”


PRESENTATION TASK — GROUP 4


1) WHO IS THE AUTHOR?
Jeffrey Abt is a scholar of museum history, visual culture and collecting. His approach combines museum studies, art history and institutional history. In this chapter he studies the genealogy of the public museum rather than individual artworks.


Suggested spoken version:
“Abt approaches museums as historical institutions. His key question is not simply when museums opened to the public, but how ownership, access, authority and civic purpose came to be combined under the category of the ‘public museum’.”


2) CLEAR SUMMARY OF THE ARTICLE
Suggested spoken version:
“Abt argues that the public museum did not suddenly emerge in the Enlightenment as a fully democratic institution. It developed through a much longer history, from classical civic display and Renaissance princely collections to Enlightenment classification, revolutionary nationalisation and nineteenth-century philanthropy. His most important point is that ‘public’ is not a single condition. A museum can be publicly accessible while remaining privately governed, or nationally owned while its interpretive authority remains concentrated in specialists and elites. The article therefore separates public access from public authority.”


3) QUOTED PARAGRAPHS / DISCUSSION
Use the visual quote cards inserted below.


QUOTE CARD 1
“least-questioned expressions” — p. 115
Why discuss it:
Abt begins by destabilising the phrase “public museum” itself. The interesting question is not only what a museum contains, but why we accept the category “public” so easily.


Discussion:
What actually makes a museum public?


QUOTE CARD 2
“social as well as physical space” — p. 127
Why discuss it:
As access expands, the museum becomes more than a building. It becomes a social institution where audiences, classes and knowledge systems encounter one another.


Discussion:
Can broader access be called democratic if interpretive authority remains centralised?


QUOTE CARD 3
“public service, education, and social stability” — p. 131
Why discuss it:
Nineteenth-century American museums often combined private governance with public civic claims.


Discussion:
Can private philanthropy genuinely serve the public without reproducing elite power?


QUOTE CARD 4
“steadily evolving institutional form” — p. 132
Why discuss it:
This phrase helps reject a teleological story in which museums naturally progress from private to public to democratic.


Discussion:
If publicness is always changing, what should count as a genuinely public museum today?

TONY BENNETT — “THE EXHIBITIONARY COMPLEX” (1988)
New Formations, no. 4, pp. 73–102


MAIN IDEA
Bennett extends Foucault’s account of modern power. Foucault’s classic institutions — prison, clinic, asylum, school — discipline individuals through surveillance, enclosure and normalization. Bennett argues that museums, exhibitions, fairs and related public institutions form another apparatus of power: the “exhibitionary complex.”


This complex governs by making things, populations and social order visible.


The key move:
modern power operates not only through surveillance but also through spectacle.


1. EXHIBITIONARY COMPLEX
CONCEPT — exhibitionary complex
Meaning: a network of museums, exhibitions, world fairs and related institutions that organise objects and people through public display.


These institutions:
• classify
• arrange
• compare
• narrate progress
• make social hierarchies visible
• train visitors in public behaviour


The exhibition is therefore not neutral.
It is a political technology of visibility.


Strong formula:
“The exhibitionary complex makes power visible by turning the world into an ordered display.”


2. BENNETT + FOUCAULT
Foucault:
prison / clinic / asylum → enclosure, discipline, surveillance.


Bennett:
museum / exhibition / fair → visibility, spectacle, classification.


Bennett does not reject Foucault.
He supplements him.


Strong seminar line:
“Bennett extends Foucault by showing that modern power operates not only through confinement and surveillance, but also through public display.”


3. PANOPTICON VS EXHIBITION
Panopticon:
few observe many.


Exhibitionary complex:
many observe objects, social order and one another.


The difference is crucial:
the crowd itself becomes visible.


Bennett’s exact phrase:
“making the crowd itself the ultimate spectacle.”


USE FOR:
self-regulation, social visibility, the visitor as part of the display.


4. SEEING AND BEING SEEN
One of Bennett’s strongest ideas:
visitors do not simply look at objects.


They also:
• observe other visitors
• become observable themselves
• learn codes of behaviour
• monitor themselves in public


This produces a self-regulating public.


Bennett describes the exhibition as producing:
“a society watching over itself.”


USE FOR:
museum etiquette, public conduct, surveillance, self-discipline.


5. SELF-REGULATION
Museum behaviour appears voluntary:
people lower their voices, follow routes, avoid touching, respect barriers.


But Bennett asks:
How are these behaviours socially produced?


The museum teaches visitors to internalise norms.


This is Foucauldian power:
effective power does not always need direct coercion.
People begin to regulate themselves.


Strong line:
“The museum disciplines without looking like a disciplinary institution.”


6. PUBLICNESS IS A TECHNOLOGY
Museums are often narrated as democratic because they open collections to the public.


Bennett complicates this.


Public access can also be a technique of government:
the institution gathers people into ordered spaces, exposes them to classifications and trains them in particular forms of conduct.


So:
public ≠ automatically democratic.


Strong question:
“What kind of public does the museum produce?”


7. MUSEUMS PRODUCE CITIZENS
The nineteenth-century museum was linked to projects of civic education.


Visitors were expected to become:
• rational
• orderly
• educable
• respectable
• self-disciplined


Museum culture therefore participated in making a modern citizen.


Important:
the museum does not simply receive an already-existing public.
It helps constitute one.


Strong formula:
“The museum is not only for the public; it is one of the institutions through which ‘the public’ is made.”


8. THE GREAT EXHIBITION, 1851
One of Bennett’s key historical examples:
The Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace, London, 1851.


What was displayed:
• industrial production
• technology
• commodities
• imperial resources
• national achievements


Why it matters:
the world appears collected, ordered and visible inside one space.


The exhibition presents modernity as something that can be surveyed.


Historical process:
industrial capitalism + imperial expansion + new technologies of display + mass public spectatorship.


9. PROGRESS AS DISPLAY
Nineteenth-century exhibitions often arranged cultures, technologies and objects as stages of development.


This creates a temporal hierarchy:
primitive → civilised
traditional → modern
simple → advanced


Classification becomes a story of progress.


Strong point:
space is used to represent historical time.


A visitor can literally walk through an ideology of development.


10. CLASSIFICATION IS POWER
The exhibitionary complex does not simply collect objects.
It puts them into relationships.


Categories decide:
• what belongs together
• what is separate
• what is advanced
• what is primitive
• what counts as art
• what counts as ethnography
• what counts as technology


Strong formula:
“Classification turns difference into order.”


Connection to Foucault:
knowledge and power operate together because classification makes the world governable and intelligible.


11. IMPERIALISM
Bennett’s argument is particularly important for colonial museums and world fairs.


Imperial display could bring colonised peoples, objects and resources into a European visual order.


The metropolitan viewer occupied the position from which this world could be surveyed.


This creates an asymmetry:
some people classify;
others are classified.


Some look;
others are rendered visible as objects of knowledge.


Strong line:
“The exhibitionary gaze universalises the viewpoint of those who possess the authority to classify.”


12. CIVILISED / PRIMITIVE
Victorian displays frequently embedded racial and civilisational hierarchies in spatial organisation.


Non-European peoples and objects could be positioned as:
• earlier
• traditional
• exotic
• less developed


while European industrial modernity represented the present or future.


Important:
this hierarchy could appear objective because it was materialised through display.


The room itself makes ideology look factual.


13. SPECTACLE + SURVEILLANCE
Bennett’s key theoretical contribution:
spectacle and surveillance are not opposites.


The exhibition combines them.


People come because they want to see.
But the architecture also makes them visible.


This is why Bennett’s exhibitionary complex is not simply the reverse of the Panopticon.


It combines:
• panoramic vision
• public spectacle
• mutual observation
• self-regulation


14. ARCHITECTURE AS GOVERNMENT
Architecture matters.


Viewing platforms, balconies, galleries, circulation routes and open sightlines organise who can see what.


Historical examples:
• Crystal Palace
• Eiffel Tower at the 1889 Paris Exposition
• exhibition galleries
• department stores


These provide elevated positions from which crowds and displays can be surveyed.


Strong point:
vision is spatially engineered.


15. “YOU ARE PART OF THE SHOW”
Bennett quotes an instruction from the 1901 Pan-American Exposition:
“you are part of the show.”


Why this matters:
the visitor is simultaneously spectator and spectacle.


The exhibitionary public learns to see itself as an ordered collective.


This is not simply entertainment.
It is social pedagogy.


16. ORDERED CROWD VS DANGEROUS CROWD
Nineteenth-century political elites often treated crowds as potentially disorderly.


The exhibition helps produce another model:
the orderly public.


Instead of:
mob / disorder / riot


the exhibition offers:
visitor / citizen / spectator.


Strong line:
“The exhibition transforms the politically dangerous crowd into a culturally regulated public.”


17. MUSEUM AND FAIR
Bennett also discusses tension between:
official educational exhibition
and
popular fair / amusement.


Fairs could include:
• entertainment
• bodily spectacle
• illicit pleasures
• commercial attractions


Authorities repeatedly tried to regulate these spaces and make entertainment compatible with educational and moral aims.


This shows:
the exhibitionary complex was never perfectly controlled.


Important:
power is contested, not total.


18. WHY BENNETT IS NOT SAYING “MUSEUMS ARE BAD”
Do not reduce the argument to:
museum = oppression.


Bennett’s question is institutional:
What forms of power become possible through public exhibition?


Museums can democratise access AND govern behaviour at the same time.


These are not mutually exclusive.


Strong seminar line:
“Bennett’s argument is strongest when we resist treating democratisation and discipline as opposites.”


19. CONNECTION TO ABT
Abt:
How did private collections become public museums?


Bennett:
What political work does this new public visibility perform?


Abt gives institutional history.
Bennett gives a theory of government through exhibition.


Strong synthesis:
“The shift from private collection to public museum expands access but also creates new possibilities for organising the public.”


20. CONNECTION TO MARTIN BECK
Beck:
display structures meaning.


Bennett:
display also structures subjects.


So:
display organises objects AND visitors.


Strong synthesis:
“Beck asks what display does to objects; Bennett asks what exhibition does to publics.”


21. CONNECTION TO FOUCAULT — POWER/KNOWLEDGE
Foucault:
knowledge creates categories that support power.


Bennett:
museums spatialise those categories.


Classification becomes visible, walkable and apparently natural.


Strong line:
“The exhibition materialises a regime of knowledge.”


22. CONNECTION TO TROUILLOT
Trouillot:
power shapes which histories become sources, archives and narratives.


Bennett:
exhibition gives selected narratives public visibility.


Therefore:
display is one of the final sites where historical authority becomes material and public.


Strong synthesis:
“Trouillot explains how a narrative becomes possible; Bennett explains how institutions make that narrative publicly authoritative.”


23. CONNECTION TO MASSEY
Massey:
place identity is relational and historically constructed.


Bennett:
institutions can spatially organise particular versions of identity.


Example:
national museums produce a spatial narrative of the nation by choosing what belongs inside national history.


24. CONNECTION TO HARVEY
Harvey:
capital and urbanisation reorganise space.


Bennett:
modern exhibition spaces reorganise visibility and public conduct.


World exhibitions are ideal sites for combining the two:
capital, commodities, technological progress and imperial power become spectacle.


25. BRITISH MUSEUM APPLICATION
Use Bennett to analyse the Enlightenment Gallery.


Questions:
• How is knowledge spatially ordered?
• What type of viewer is imagined?
• Which objects represent civilisation, science or progress?
• Who historically had the authority to classify?
• Does public access challenge authority, or reproduce it?
• How does the gallery turn classification into something visually persuasive?


Strong application:
“The gallery does not simply contain Enlightenment knowledge; it performs the Enlightenment fantasy that the world can be collected, ordered and surveyed.”


26. CONTEMPORARY APPLICATION
Bennett still works today.


Think about:
• blockbuster exhibitions
• art fairs
• immersive exhibitions
• museums designed for Instagram
• branded cultural spaces
• digital visitor tracking
• AI-generated interpretation


The basic question remains:
How do institutions organise seeing and being seen?


27. AI + THE EXHIBITIONARY COMPLEX
Useful for your semester project.


If AI companies enter cultural institutions as:
• sponsors
• infrastructure providers
• educational partners
• interpretation tools


then they can become part of the exhibitionary apparatus.


Foucauldian question:
Who produces authoritative knowledge?


Bennett question:
How is that authority made publicly visible and normal?


Strong project line:
“If the museum is an exhibitionary technology, corporate sponsorship can participate in the staging of legitimacy itself.”


28. EXACT QUOTES FOR ESSAYS
Use short verified quotations and analyse them.


1. “making the crowd itself the ultimate spectacle.”
USE FOR: exhibition, visibility, self-regulation.


2. “a society watching over itself.”
USE FOR: mutual surveillance and the self-regulating public.


3. “you are part of the show.”
Bennett cites this instruction from the 1901 Pan-American Exposition.
USE FOR: visitor as spectator and spectacle.


QUOTE RULE:
CLAIM → QUOTE → ANALYSIS.


Example:
Bennett argues that exhibitionary architecture does not merely expose objects to viewers; it also exposes viewers to one another. His phrase “making the crowd itself the ultimate spectacle” captures the way exhibitionary space transforms spectators into visible social subjects. The political effect is self-regulation: visitors monitor both themselves and others within a publicly staged order.


29. WHAT TO SAY IN A SEMINAR
“Bennett extends Foucault’s analysis of disciplinary institutions by showing that public exhibitions constitute another technology of power, one based on spectacle, visibility and classification.”


“The museum does not simply make objects public. It makes a particular social order publicly visible.”


“The exhibitionary complex transforms the visitor into both observer and observed, producing forms of self-regulation through public visibility.”


“Classification in the museum is not only epistemological; it is spatial and political.”


30. HYPER-INTELLECTUAL LINES
“The exhibitionary complex converts epistemic hierarchy into spatial experience.”


“Visibility is not the opposite of power; in Bennett, visibility is one of power’s techniques.”


“The museum’s democratic promise of access is inseparable from its governmental capacity to organise conduct.”


“Exhibition transforms knowledge into spectacle and spectacle into pedagogy.”


“The visitor is governed not simply by being watched, but by being incorporated into a social field of mutual visibility.”


FINAL FORMULA
BENNETT = MODERN POWER DOES NOT ONLY HIDE, CONFINE AND WATCH. IT ALSO DISPLAYS, CLASSIFIES AND INVITES THE PUBLIC TO WATCH ITSELF.


For museum studies:
analyse objects, but also analyse the architecture of visibility, the categories of display, the behaviour expected from visitors, and the political image of society that the exhibition stages.


SOURCE
Tony Bennett, “The Exhibitionary Complex,” New Formations, no. 4 (Spring 1988), pp. 73–102.
Assigned PDF: https://www.columbia.edu/itc/anthropology/schildkrout/6353/client_edit/week1/bennett.pdf
”

WEEK 3 MUSEUM VISIT — GROUP 4
British Museum: Room 1, Enlightenment Gallery


WHY THIS DISPLAY?
We chose the Enlightenment Gallery because it lets us analyse the British Museum not simply as a container of historical objects but as a historical object in itself.
The room stages the conditions in which the Museum emerged:
• Enlightenment collecting
• classification
• universal knowledge
• expanding imperial networks
• changing definitions of “the public”


This connects directly to Abt: the history of museums is a history of changing relationships between private ownership, public access, knowledge and political authority.


FOCUS: HANS SLOANE
Sloane’s private collection became one of the foundations of the British Museum.
This appears as a progressive story:
private collection → public institution → national knowledge.
But it is more complicated.
Sloane’s collecting was connected to colonial Jamaica and imperial networks.
Therefore the “universal” collection depends on very unequal conditions of movement, extraction and possession.


MAIN THESIS FOR THE TOUR
The Enlightenment museum is simultaneously an institution of democratisation and an institution of epistemic authority: it expands access to knowledge while concentrating the power to classify that knowledge.


WHAT IS THE DISPLAY ABOUT?
At the simplest level: how eighteenth-century Europeans collected, compared and classified objects to make the world knowable.
Objects from different cultures and periods become organised through categories such as:
material
type
chronology
function


Collecting → classification → comparison → hierarchy → knowledge.


Strong formulation:
The museum does not simply collect knowledge; it produces knowledge through classification.


HOW TO ANALYSE IT


1. SPACE & ARCHITECTURE
Room 1 looks ordered, rational, encyclopaedic.
Its architecture makes Enlightenment knowledge appear coherent and authoritative.
It was historically King George III’s Library.
This allows a direct Abt reading:
royal knowledge → national knowledge.
Architecture performs a political transformation in ownership and legitimacy.


2. CLASSIFICATION & KNOWLEDGE
Classification is not neutral.
To classify is to decide what counts as similarity, difference, chronology, civilisation and value.
Connection to Foucault:
classification is epistemic power.
A museum makes categories look natural by materialising them spatially.


3. OWNERSHIP → PUBLICNESS
Sloane’s private collection becomes national property.
But ask:
Did ownership become public?
Did interpretation become public?
Did authorship of knowledge become public?
Strong line:
Public ownership does not necessarily mean public authorship of knowledge.


4. EMPIRE & GLOBAL NETWORKS
Enlightenment knowledge and British imperial expansion occur together.
Avoid the simplistic claim “Enlightenment = colonialism”.
The stronger claim is:
Imperial infrastructures were among the material conditions that made universal collecting possible.
Ships, merchants, colonial administrators, missionaries and plantations enabled objects and information to travel to London.


Connection to Massey:
power-geometry.
Who has the power to move through the world, collect it, extract from it and classify it?


5. AUDIENCE
The museum does not merely open itself to a pre-existing public.
It helps produce a particular public:
educated
rational
orderly
self-regulating
capable of appreciating objects through institutional categories.


Connection to Bennett:
exhibitionary complex.


OBJECT 1 — SLOANE ASTROLABE
Why useful:
An English medieval scientific instrument embodying Arabic astronomical knowledge.
It disrupts a purely European story of scientific progress.
Even within a British collection, knowledge is already transnational.
Question:
If knowledge has always circulated across cultures, what does it mean for a national museum to organise it as British heritage?


OBJECT 2 — GRAY’S INN LANE HANDAXE
Part of Sloane’s collection.
Its interpretation changes as archaeological knowledge develops.
Object remains physically similar; epistemology changes.
Question:
Does a museum preserve an object’s meaning, or continually produce new meanings for it?


FINAL QUESTION FOR THE GROUP
Can a museum genuinely claim to represent universal knowledge if the categories through which that knowledge is organised emerged from a particular European and imperial history?


3–4 MINUTE SCRIPT


We chose Room 1, the Enlightenment Gallery, focusing on Hans Sloane’s collection and the classification of knowledge. We chose it because the room allows us to examine the British Museum not just as a place containing historical objects, but as a historical institution produced by Enlightenment ideas of collecting, classification and public knowledge. It connects directly to Jeffrey Abt’s argument that the public museum emerged through changing relationships between private property, civic authority and access.


What interests us most is that the gallery presents collecting as a way of making the world knowable. Objects from very different cultures and periods were removed from their original contexts, catalogued and reorganised according to categories such as material, type, chronology or function. Classification therefore does not simply describe the world; it produces a particular order of knowledge.


Sloane is especially interesting because his private collection became one of the foundations of the British Museum in 1753. This can be read as a democratisation of knowledge: private possession was transformed into a national public collection. But Abt makes us question what “public” actually means. Public access does not necessarily mean public control over interpretation. The Museum still determines how objects are classified, narrated and valued.


We also need to place this Enlightenment project within imperial history. Sloane’s collecting was connected to colonial Jamaica, while Britain’s expanding imperial networks made the movement of objects and knowledge to London possible. Empire therefore should not be treated simply as the historical background of the Museum; it was one of the material conditions through which the idea of universal collecting could operate.


Finally, the room itself matters. It was built as King George III’s Library, later presented to the nation. Architecturally, it performs a transition from royal knowledge to national knowledge. But this raises our central question: when knowledge becomes “public”, who still retains the authority to organise it?


So rather than asking only what these objects tell us about the eighteenth century, we want to ask what the display tells us about the construction of the museum itself: who collects, who classifies, who owns, and who gets to speak for the public.




QUOTE CARD 1 — Questioning “public museum”
  



QUOTE CARD 2 — Museum as social space
  



QUOTE CARD 3 — Civic mission
  



QUOTE CARD 4 — The museum keeps evolving

────────

2) WHAT IS THE DISPLAY ABOUT?
The Enlightenment Gallery shows how eighteenth-century European collectors attempted to make the world knowable through collecting, classification and comparison.


Core sequence:

Strong line:
“The display is therefore not only about what Enlightenment Europeans knew. It is about how knowledge itself was produced.”


3) HOW TO ANALYSE IT
Analyse through five layers:


A. SPACE & ARCHITECTURE
The room’s order, symmetry and library-like architecture make knowledge appear rational, comprehensive and authoritative.


Important historical fact:

Strong line:

This is not neutral storage; classification creates relationships and hierarchy.

C. OWNERSHIP → PUBLICNESS

Question:

The objects? Access? Ownership? Interpretation?

D. EMPIRE & GLOBAL NETWORKS
Enlightenment collecting depended on imperial routes, merchants, colonial administrators, military expeditions and unequal mobility.

“Empire was not merely the dark background to Enlightenment collecting; imperial networks were among the material conditions that made such collecting possible.”


Connection to Massey:
This is a museum version of power-geometry: some actors had far greater power to move, extract, collect and classify.


E. AUDIENCE & THE PUBLIC
The museum does not simply receive visitors; it creates a model of the visitor — rational, educated, orderly and capable of appreciating objects through institutional categories.

the exhibitionary complex.

“The museum did not simply open knowledge to an already existing public; it helped construct a particular kind of public.”


KEY OBJECT 1 — SLOANE ASTROLABE

“If knowledge has always circulated across cultures, what does it mean for a national museum to organise that knowledge as British heritage?”

Why useful:
The object’s physical form stays the same while archaeological interpretation changes over time.


Strong line:
“Objects do not have fixed meanings; museums produce new meanings as knowledge systems evolve.”


CENTRAL THESIS FOR THE VISIT

David Harvey — “The Right to the City” (2012)
Rebel Cities, pp. 17–38


Главная идея
Право на город — это не просто право пользоваться городскими ресурсами. Это коллективное право влиять на то, как город производится, перестраивается и кому достаются выгоды от этого процесса.


1. Right to the city = collective right
Harvey спорит с индивидуалистическим пониманием городских прав. Недостаточно иметь доступ к паркам, транспорту или жилью; важнее вопрос, кто реально принимает решения о развитии города.
Ключевая формула: право на город = коллективная власть над процессом urbanisation.


2. Urbanisation absorbs surplus capital
Капитализм постоянно производит surplus capital — избыточный капитал, который нужно реинвестировать. Строительство городов, инфраструктуры, жилья, дорог и коммерческих зон становится одним из главных способов этот капитал поглощать.
То есть город — не фон экономики, а один из механизмов capitalist accumulation.


3. Haussmann и Париж
После кризиса 1848 года масштабная перестройка Парижа при Haussmann поглощает капитал и рабочую силу.
Но одновременно:
• старые районы разрушаются;
• часть рабочего населения вытесняется;
• растёт стоимость центральной земли;
• появляются новые пространства consumption — boulevards, cafés, department stores.
Вывод: urban redevelopment одновременно экономический, социальный и политический процесс.


4. Robert Moses и Нью-Йорк
В XX веке похожую роль играет suburbanisation США: highways, suburbs, housing.
Это создаёт спрос не только на строительство, но и на автомобили, бытовую технику, мебель, топливо.
Urban form производит определённый lifestyle и поддерживает consumption.


5. Creative destruction
Капитализм перестраивает город через “creative destruction”: создание нового пространства требует уничтожения или вытеснения старого.
Важно всегда спрашивать:
• что создаётся?
• что уничтожается?
• кто выигрывает?
• кто платит цену?


6. Dispossession
Harvey связывает urban development с dispossession — потерей земли, жилья, public space или доступа к ресурсам.
Пример: social housing / affordable neighbourhood → redevelopment → рост стоимости земли → displacement старых жителей.


7. Gentrification
Gentrification у Harvey — не просто смена “атмосферы района”. Это процесс, где коллективно созданная urban value может быть присвоена частными владельцами недвижимости и investors.
Сильная формула: collective social life creates value, but private actors often capture the financial gain.


8. Use value vs exchange value
Housing имеет:
• use value — место для жизни;
• exchange value — asset, который можно купить, продать, сдавать и использовать для инвестиций.
Проблема возникает, когда exchange value начинает доминировать над social need.


9. Financialisation
Современная urbanisation тесно связана с banks, credit, mortgages и debt.
Физический город становится связан с глобальными financial flows.
Housing bubble 2008 показывает, что urbanisation может не только поглощать капитал, но и производить кризисы.


10. Spatial fix
Важный Harvey-концепт.
Капитал временно “решает” проблему избытка, вкладываясь в пространство: roads, housing, infrastructure.
Но одновременно капитал фиксируется в built environment и создаёт новые ограничения.
Spatial fix = временное решение, которое может породить следующий кризис.


11. Regeneration for whom?
Harvey заставляет подозревать нейтральные слова вроде “regeneration”.
Любой redevelopment нужно анализировать через вопросы:
• who finances it?
• who controls it?
• who captures the uplift in land value?
• who is displaced?
• who gets access to the new city?


12. Democracy vs property
Индивидуальное право собственности может конфликтовать с коллективным right to the city.
Если тысячи частных решений повышают rent и вытесняют жителей, юридически всё может быть “нормально”, но политически возникает вопрос о том, кто контролирует urban transformation.


13. The city produces us
Город не только создаётся людьми — он формирует их образ жизни.
Car-based suburbia производит car dependency.
Dense city + public transport производит другую модель mobility.
Gated communities, malls и public squares создают разные формы social life.


14. Neoliberal city
Проблема Harvey не в том, что “государство исчезло”.
Наоборот, государство активно участвует через zoning, infrastructure, incentives, privatisation.
Вопрос в том, чьи интересы обслуживает связка state + market.


15. Главный политический вывод
Right to the city = greater democratic control over the production and use of urban surplus.
То есть вопрос не только “как выглядит город?”, а “кто контролирует ресурсы, которые его производят?”


Примеры для семинара
King’s Cross — regeneration, rising land value, private/public investment, new cultural and corporate uses.
Elephant & Castle — redevelopment + displacement local traders and communities.
Canary Wharf — urban space as infrastructure for finance.
Shoreditch — cultural value created collectively, then monetised through property and investment.


Что важно сказать на семинаре
• Harvey не просто говорит, что капитализм влияет на город; город — один из механизмов воспроизводства капитала.
• Он не спорит против любых изменений; вопрос — кто контролирует transformation и кто получает выгоду.
• Urban crisis нельзя свести только к planning failures: housing inequality, gentrification и displacement встроены в political economy города.


Сильные формулировки
“The city is not merely shaped by capital; it is one of the infrastructures through which capital reproduces itself.”
“Regeneration is never only spatial improvement; it is also a redistribution of value and power.”
“The conflict is not between change and preservation, but between different actors’ capacity to control urban transformation.

DAVID HARVEY — “THE RIGHT TO THE CITY” (2012)
1. “It is, moreover, a collective rather than an individual right.” (Harvey, 2012, p. 4)
USE FOR: right to the city as collective power rather than individual access.
2. “Capitalism needs urbanization to absorb the surplus products it perpetually produces.” (Harvey, 2012, p. 5)
USE FOR: the structural relationship between capitalist accumulation and urbanisation.

materials.userNotes:
Doreen Massey — “Places and their Pasts” (1995)
History Workshop Journal, 39, pp. 182–192


Главная идея
Massey спорит с представлением о месте как о закрытой территории с одной стабильной идентичностью и одним “настоящим” прошлым. Для неё place — это временная, постоянно меняющаяся конфигурация социальных отношений, связей, миграций, конфликтов и историй. У места не один past, а множество pasts.


1. Place is relational, not bounded
Место определяется не только тем, что находится внутри его физических границ. Его идентичность создаётся отношениями, которые проходят через него и связывают его с другими местами.
Пример: London невозможно понять как изолированный “английский” город. Его форма и идентичность исторически производились через imperial trade, migration, finance, ports, labour and global networks.
Исторический пример: East London и Docklands формировались как часть портовой экономики Британской империи. Товары, люди и капитал, приходившие из колониальных и международных сетей, были не “внешним влиянием”, а частью производства самого места.


ПОНЯТИЕ — relational place
Откуда исходит: более широкая пространственная теория Massey, развитая в её работах конца 1980-х–1990-х, особенно в “A Global Sense of Place” (1991) и Space, Place and Gender (1994).
Что значит: идентичность места возникает из отношений, а не из внутренней неизменной essence.


2. Pasts во множественном числе
Название “Places and their Pasts” принципиально. Одно место может одновременно иметь рабочую, миграционную, колониальную, гендерную, индустриальную, религиозную и элитарную историю.
Пример: Brixton можно читать как историю Afro-Caribbean migration; policing and uprisings; music and nightlife; housing; gentrification. Нельзя выбрать одну из этих историй и объявить её всей “историей Brixton”.


3. Critique of authenticity
Massey подозрительно относится к фразам “настоящий район”, “традиционная культура”, “подлинная идентичность места”.
Почему: любой момент, который объявляют “аутентичным”, сам был результатом более ранних изменений.
Пример: Soho сегодня часто романтизируют как “старый богемный London”. Но его идентичность веками формировалась через Huguenot, Italian, Jewish, Chinese, queer and entertainment histories. “Чистого” исходного Soho, от которого потом началось смешение, практически невозможно выделить.


ПОНЯТИЕ — anti-essentialism
Откуда исходит: более широкий постструктуралистский и феминистский поворот в гуманитарных науках XX века; у Massey это означает отказ считать место обладателем вечной внутренней сущности.
Полезная формула: difference does not require purity.


4. Nostalgia as politics
Ностальгия становится политической, когда один период прошлого объявляется золотым стандартом, а последующие изменения — decline или contamination.
Вопрос Massey: почему именно этот момент считается “настоящим”?
Пример: “раньше East End был настоящим working-class London”. Но сам working-class East End был сформирован миграцией, портовой экономикой, imperial trade и внутренними перемещениями населения.


5. Identity is contested
У места нет одного коллективного голоса. Разные группы производят разные версии его identity.
Пример: для Brixton один и тот же район может быть:
• home для long-term residents;
• символ Black British history;
• nightlife destination;
• investment opportunity для developer;
• “up-and-coming area” для estate agent.
Эти значения существуют одновременно и конфликтуют.


6. Global sense of place
Local и global не являются противоположностями. Локальная специфика часто появляется именно из глобальных связей.
Пример: Venice уникальна не потому, что была изолирована, а потому что исторически была узлом Mediterranean trade, отношений с Byzantine и Islamic worlds, maritime capitalism и migration.


ПОНЯТИЕ — global sense of place
Откуда исходит: эссе Massey “A Global Sense of Place” (1991).
Что значит: открытость внешним связям не уничтожает уникальность места. Уникальность — это особая комбинация этих связей.


7. Power-geometry
Не все люди одинаково включены в mobility и global flows.
Один человек контролирует движение капитала и свободно летает между global cities; другой движется из-за войны, работы или миграционной необходимости и зависит от виз, border regimes и работодателей.


ПОНЯТИЕ — power-geometry
Откуда исходит: концепт Massey начала 1990-х, особенно связанный с её текстом “Power-geometry and a progressive sense of place” (1993).
Что значит: пространство и мобильность организованы неравномерно; разные группы имеют разную степень контроля над потоками людей, денег, информации и товаров.
Пример: Heathrow для business executive может означать connectivity and freedom; для asylum seeker — border control, restriction and surveillance. Одно место, разные позиции внутри географии власти.


8. Place as process
Place не является законченной сущностью. Оно постоянно производится.
Это сильнее, чем просто “места меняются”: изменение не разрушает исходную идентичность, потому что никакой полностью фиксированной исходной идентичности не существует.
Полезная формула: change does not happen to place from outside; change is part of how place exists.


9. Heritage is selective
Heritage не просто сохраняет прошлое — он выбирает, какое прошлое делать видимым.
Вопросы:
• что получает plaque, museum, conservation status?
• что остаётся без архива?
• чья история становится “характером района”?
Исторический пример: industrial districts после deindustrialisation часто сохраняют brick façades, factory names и warehouse aesthetics, хотя рабочая инфраструктура и communities исчезают.


10. The past can become a market asset
Очень сильная связка с Harvey.
Бывшую фабрику превращают в luxury lofts, но сохраняют industrial typography, exposed brick и название “The Foundry”.
Экономически произошло displacement и смена собственности; символически working-class past сохраняется как branding.
Сильная формула: the people may be displaced while their history is retained as branding.


11. Representation produces place
Карта, музей, выставка, tourist guide, urban branding не просто описывают место — они участвуют в производстве его identity.
Пример: выставка про East End, которая показывает Victorian markets и Cockney culture, но исключает Jewish, Bangladeshi и colonial histories, не просто “неполна”; она создаёт определённую версию East End.


Связка с Martin Beck:
Beck: display produces meaning.
Massey: representations of place participate in producing place.
Следовательно, выставка о районе — не нейтральное отражение района, а активный агент в politics of place.


12. Belonging ≠ ownership
Связь с местом не обязательно даёт моральную монополию на него.
Фраза “мы здесь были раньше, значит это наше настоящее место” у Massey требует критики, потому что почти любое место имеет историю перемещений, контактов и конфликтов.
Это особенно важно для nationalism, migration and heritage politics.


13. Multiple histories do not mean relativism
Massey не говорит, что “истин нет” и любая версия прошлого одинаково верна.
Факты можно проверять.
Но превращение отдельных фактов в целостную identity места неизбежно selective.
То есть multiplicity ≠ anything goes.


14. Non-teleological history
Настоящее не является неизбежным итогом прошлого.
Когда сегодняшний financial district описывают так, будто он “всегда шёл” к нынешней форме, это задним числом превращает политические решения и случайности в destiny.
Пример: Canary Wharf — не естественный финал Docklands. Его появление зависело от deregulation, state policy, infrastructure, finance and redevelopment decisions.


ПОНЯТИЕ — teleology
Откуда исходит: философия истории.
Teleological narrative объясняет прошлое так, будто оно неизбежно двигалось к сегодняшнему результату.
Почему Massey это ломает: place имеет множество возможных траекторий, а настоящее — лишь одна из них.


15. Colonial relations constitute the metropolis
Очень важный интеллектуальный вывод: империя — не просто внешняя история, которая “повлияла” на London.
Colonial relations участвовали в производстве самого metropolis: wealth, institutions, architecture, commodities, population and culture.
То есть colony и metropolis нельзя мыслить как полностью отдельные сущности.


16. Главное, что спросить у любого place narrative
• Who is defining this place?
• Which past is being selected?
• Which histories disappear?
• Which external relations made this place possible?
• Who is mobile and who is constrained?
• Who benefits from the current version of “local identity”?


Что сказать на семинаре
• Massey replaces territorial identity with relational identity.
• A place can be highly specific without being pure or closed.
• The politics of place is partly a politics of historical selection.
• Openness does not eliminate identity; it helps constitute it.
• “Local” should not be romanticised as the opposite of “global”.


Сильные формулировки
“Place is not a container of history but a temporary constellation of relations.”
“A relational account of place replaces authenticity with specificity: a place can be unique without being pure.”
“The political question is not simply what happened here, but who gets to organise particular pasts into the identity of the place.”
“Massey shifts the question from ‘what is the true identity of this place?’ to ‘through which relations, exclusions and narratives is this place being made intelligible as a particular place?’”


Связка Harvey + Massey
Harvey asks: who controls urban transformation and who captures value?
Massey asks: who defines the identity of place and which pasts become visible?
Вместе они позволяют анализировать gentrification одновременно как материальное перераспределение земли/капитала и как символическое переписывание памяти района.
”

DOREEN MASSEY — “PLACES AND THEIR PASTS” (1995)
1. “The identity of places is very much bound up with the histories which are told of them.” (Massey, 1995, p. 186)
USE FOR: place identity as narratively and historically constructed.
2. “so too does the present make the past.” (Massey, 1995, p. 188)
USE FOR: the present actively reorganises and interprets the past rather than simply inheriting it.
