MICHEL FOUCAULT — “7th January 1976”
Society Must Be Defended: Lectures at the Collège de France 1975–76, pp. 1–21
MAIN IDEA
This lecture is not a finished theory of power. It is Foucault explaining how he wants to study power historically: not through one universal theory, but through local struggles, marginalised knowledges, discontinuities and conflicts.
The central move:
Foucault is suspicious of “total” theories that claim to explain everything from above. He prefers genealogy — a method that reconstructs how particular systems of knowledge and power emerged through struggle, contingency and exclusion.
1. WHY FOUCAULT IS CRITICAL OF GRAND THEORY
Foucault begins by reflecting on the previous decade of intellectual work. He argues that many useful critiques were effective precisely because they were local and specific rather than totalising.
Examples of the kind of struggles he has in mind:
• psychiatry and the institution of the asylum
• prisons and penal systems
• sexuality
• medical authority
• institutions that define what counts as normal or deviant
He is not saying theory is useless. He is saying that a single theory can become too smooth and suppress difference.
PONЯТИЕ — totalising theory
Origin: twentieth-century philosophy and social theory; in Foucault, a target of critique.
Meaning: a theoretical system that tries to explain social reality as one coherent whole.
Why Foucault resists it: it can erase contradiction, local histories and forms of knowledge that do not fit the dominant framework.
Strong seminar line:
“Foucault is not rejecting theory; he is rejecting the idea that one theoretical system should have the final authority to organise every struggle.”
2. SUBJUGATED KNOWLEDGES
This is one of the most important concepts in the lecture.
PONЯТИЕ — subjugated knowledges
Meaning: forms of knowledge that have been buried, disqualified, dismissed as naïve, unscientific, low-status or irrelevant.
Foucault uses the term in two senses:
1) historical contents that have been masked or buried inside formal systems;
2) local, experiential knowledges that official institutions treat as inferior.
Examples:
• patients’ knowledge of psychiatric institutions
• prisoners’ knowledge of prisons
• nurses’ practical knowledge compared with medical hierarchy
• colonised communities’ knowledge compared with imperial classification
• workers’ knowledge compared with managerial expertise
Important:
He is NOT saying that marginal knowledge is automatically true.
The point is that institutions decide which knowledge counts as legitimate.
Strong formula:
“The question is not only what is true, but who has the authority to define which knowledge is serious enough to count as truth.”
3. “INSURRECTION OF SUBJUGATED KNOWLEDGES”
Foucault describes genealogy as an “insurrection” of these subordinated knowledges against centralised theoretical authority.
This does not mean replacing one official truth with another.
It means making suppressed histories and local knowledges available for struggle.
Historical example:
The history of psychiatry changes when we stop reading only medical textbooks and also examine asylum records, institutional practices and the experiences of people classified as insane.
Museum example:
A museum may classify an object through a colonial catalogue. Genealogical analysis would ask:
• who created that category?
• what indigenous or local knowledge was excluded?
• what historical conflict made this classification authoritative?
4. GENEALOGY
PONЯТИЕ — genealogy
Origin: Friedrich Nietzsche, especially On the Genealogy of Morality; Foucault develops the method in “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971).
Genealogy asks:
How did something that now looks natural, obvious or inevitable actually come into existence?
It refuses origin stories that imagine a pure beginning.
Instead it looks for:
• accidents
• conflict
• discontinuity
• institutional struggle
• changes in language
• competing forces
• excluded alternatives
Example:
Instead of asking “When was the modern museum invented?” genealogy asks:
“How did particular practices of collecting, classification, ownership, public access and imperial acquisition gradually come together so that the modern museum became thinkable?”
This is exactly why Foucault connects well to Abt.
Strong formula:
“Genealogy turns ‘what is this?’ into ‘through what struggles did this become normal?’”
5. GENEALOGY ≠ SEARCH FOR THE TRUE ORIGIN
This is crucial.
Traditional history often looks for origins:
the first prison
the first museum
the birth of sexuality
the beginning of modernity
Foucault is suspicious of this because “origin” can make history look coherent and inevitable.
Genealogy instead reconstructs descent, accidents and ruptures.
PONЯТИЕ — anti-teleology
Meaning: refusal to tell history as if it naturally moved toward the present.
Connection to Massey:
Massey also rejects the idea that present places are inevitable outcomes of one coherent past.
Both insist on multiple trajectories and contingency.
6. ARCHAEOLOGY VS GENEALOGY
Foucault makes an important methodological distinction.
ARCHAEOLOGY:
analyses systems of discourse — what can be said, thought and classified in a particular period.
GENEALOGY:
asks how these systems are connected to struggle, power and historical conflict.
Strong shorthand:
Archaeology = mapping the rules of discourse.
Genealogy = tracing the struggles that produced and destabilise those rules.
Museum example:
Archaeology:
How did nineteenth-century museums classify “art”, “ethnography” and “natural history”?
Genealogy:
What political, colonial and institutional struggles gave those classifications authority?
7. “ANTI-SCIENCE”
Foucault calls genealogy “anti-science”, but this is easy to misunderstand.
He is NOT anti-scientific evidence.
He is attacking the political effects of a centralised discourse that claims the exclusive right to decide what counts as knowledge.
PONЯТИЕ — anti-science
Meaning in this lecture: resistance to the institutional hierarchy that ranks some knowledges as scientific and therefore authoritative while disqualifying others.
Important distinction:
Foucault is challenging the monopoly of scientific authority, not saying facts do not matter.
8. POWER IS NOT ONLY SOMETHING THE STATE POSSESSES
This lecture begins moving toward Foucault’s broader theory of power.
Traditional model:
power = law, sovereign, state, prohibition.
Foucault asks whether power should instead be analysed as something that operates through multiple relationships and institutions.
Examples:
doctor / patient
teacher / student
prison officer / prisoner
museum / visitor
expert / non-expert
This is why Foucault is useful for cultural institutions:
power operates through classification, expertise, norms and knowledge, not only through explicit force.
9. POWER / KNOWLEDGE
Although the formula “power/knowledge” is broader than this single lecture, the lecture is a clear demonstration of it.
Knowledge is not simply outside power.
Institutions produce knowledge, and knowledge helps institutions exercise authority.
Example:
Psychiatry can classify a person as “abnormal”.
That classification is knowledge, but it also changes how the person can be treated, confined or governed.
Museum example:
A museum labels an object “primitive art”, “ethnographic specimen” or “masterpiece”.
The label does not merely describe; it positions the object inside a hierarchy of knowledge.
Strong line:
“Classification is an exercise of knowledge and therefore potentially an exercise of power.”
10. FROM REPRESSION TO WAR
Toward the end of the lecture, Foucault questions two major ways of understanding power.
MODEL 1 — repression
Power works by saying no, prohibiting and suppressing.
MODEL 2 — struggle / war
Power relations may be understood as continuing historical struggle.
Foucault becomes interested in reversing Clausewitz’s famous proposition that war is the continuation of politics by other means.
He asks:
What if politics is the continuation of war by other means?
Important:
This is a methodological hypothesis, not a slogan he simply accepts without qualification.
PONЯТИЕ — Nietzsche hypothesis
Meaning: analyse power relations through struggle, confrontation and war rather than only law or repression.
11. WHY WAR?
The “war” model allows Foucault to ask whether apparently peaceful institutions preserve the outcomes of earlier struggles.
Example:
A legal or institutional order can look neutral today while embodying victories and defeats from previous conflicts.
Museum example:
A national collection may look like neutral heritage while preserving the historical outcomes of conquest, colonial acquisition, elite collecting or state appropriation.
Strong question:
“What historical victory has been made to look like neutral institutional order?”
12. HISTORY IS A BATTLEGROUND
For Foucault, history is not simply a record of what happened.
Historical narratives can legitimise institutions and power.
Who gets to tell the past affects what can be challenged in the present.
This is the strongest connection to Trouillot.
TROUILLOT CONNECTION — “THE POWER IN THE STORY”
Trouillot argues that power enters the production of history at multiple stages:
• what becomes a fact
• what enters an archive
• what is retrieved
• what becomes historically significant
Foucault:
asks which knowledges are disqualified.
Trouillot:
asks where silences enter historical production.
Together:
absence from history is not necessarily accidental; it can be socially produced.
Museum example:
An object may be carefully preserved while the history of the people who made, used or lost it is absent.
13. FOUCAULT + TROUILLOT + MUSEUMS
A strong curatorial synthesis:
Object survives.
Archive survives.
Catalogue survives.
But certain voices may not.
Therefore:
preservation does not guarantee historical completeness.
Strong seminar line:
“A museum can preserve material evidence while simultaneously reproducing historical silence.”
14. CONNECTION TO ABT
Abt:
How did the public museum historically emerge?
Foucault:
What struggles and excluded knowledges made that institutional form possible?
Abt gives genealogy-like institutional history.
Foucault gives the methodological language to analyse it.
Example:
British Museum:
Do not only ask when it became public.
Ask:
• which forms of knowledge were authorised?
• whose classifications became institutional?
• which histories of acquisition became secondary?
• what makes the institution’s categories appear neutral?
15. CONNECTION TO MASSEY
Massey:
places have multiple pasts.
Foucault:
dominant knowledge can suppress alternative histories.
Together:
a place can have many pasts, but institutions have unequal power to make some of them visible.
Strong synthesis:
“Multiplicity does not guarantee visibility; power determines which pasts acquire authority.”
16. CONNECTION TO HARVEY
Harvey focuses on material power:
capital, property, urbanisation, surplus.
Foucault focuses more on dispersed institutional power:
knowledge, expertise, norms, classification.
Useful distinction:
Harvey asks who controls resources.
Foucault asks how systems of truth make particular forms of control appear reasonable or normal.
Together:
material domination and epistemic authority can reinforce one another.
17. CONNECTION TO MARTIN BECK
Beck:
display produces meaning.
Foucault:
systems of knowledge determine what can become intelligible.
Museum display therefore does not just arrange objects visually.
It participates in a regime of knowledge.
Strong line:
“Display can function as a technology of power because it organises not only visibility, but intelligibility.”
18. HISTORICAL EXAMPLE — COLONIAL MUSEUM CLASSIFICATION
European museums historically separated collections into categories such as:
• fine art
• archaeology
• ethnography
• natural history
These categories often mapped onto assumptions about civilisation and cultural hierarchy.
European painting → “art”
colonised peoples’ objects → “ethnography”
A Foucauldian question:
Why did one object become autonomous art while another became evidence of a culture?
This is genealogy:
the category itself becomes the object of historical analysis.
19. HISTORICAL EXAMPLE — MADNESS
Foucault’s earlier work on madness is a useful example of the method.
Instead of assuming “madness” is a timeless medical object, he investigates how institutions, medicine, law and language historically produced changing definitions of madness.
The lesson:
categories that look natural may have institutional histories.
Apply to museums:
“primitive”
“authentic”
“national”
“masterpiece”
“heritage”
are also historical categories, not neutral descriptions.
20. THE MOST IMPORTANT INTELLECTUAL POINT
Foucault changes the question.
Weak question:
“Is this historical account true?”
Foucauldian additional question:
“What conditions allowed this account to become authoritative, and what alternatives did it marginalise?”
This does NOT replace evidence.
It adds analysis of authority.
WHAT TO SAY IN A SEMINAR
“Foucault’s key move in the 7 January lecture is to shift from universal theory to genealogy: the recovery of local and subjugated knowledges in order to analyse how systems of truth are historically connected to power.”
“He is not arguing that marginalised knowledge is automatically true. His concern is with the institutional mechanisms that decide which forms of knowledge are authorised and which are disqualified.”
“Genealogy does not search for a pure origin. It reconstructs contingency, struggle and discontinuity, showing that institutions which now appear natural could have developed differently.”
“A Foucauldian museum analysis would therefore ask not only what a display represents, but what system of knowledge allows its categories to appear natural.”
HYPER-INTELLECTUAL LINES
“Genealogy is less interested in recovering an authentic beginning than in denaturalising the present.”
“The political force of genealogy lies in showing that what appears necessary was historically contingent.”
“Subjugated knowledge is not simply forgotten knowledge; it is knowledge whose status has been actively downgraded within a hierarchy of credibility.”
“Power becomes most difficult to see when its historical victories have sedimented into apparently neutral categories.”
“Foucault’s target is not truth itself, but the institutional organisation of truth-authority.”
FURTHER READING CONNECTION — “NIETZSCHE, GENEALOGY, HISTORY” (1971)
Use this if you want to sound particularly strong in discussion.
Key idea:
Genealogy opposes the search for Ursprung — pure origin.
History should instead track descent, emergence, accidents and conflict.
PONЯТИЕ — Herkunft
Often translated as descent.
Focus: heterogeneous histories that compose an identity.
PONЯТИЕ — Entstehung
Emergence.
Focus: the moment when forces confront each other and a particular arrangement appears.
Why this matters:
Institutions do not emerge because history “needed” them. They emerge from specific configurations of struggle.
Museum example:
The public museum is not the inevitable endpoint of collecting. It is one historical outcome of changing relations among monarchy, state, property, science, empire, philanthropy and public access.
FURTHER READING CONNECTION — TROUILLOT, “THE POWER IN THE STORY”
Trouillot helps make Foucault more concrete.
Foucault:
Which knowledges become authorised?
Trouillot:
At what stages are alternatives silenced?
Strong combined question for curating:
“Not only whose story is displayed, but at what earlier stages did other stories become impossible to display?”
FINAL FORMULA
FOUCAULT = POWER DOES NOT ONLY CENSOR KNOWLEDGE; POWER HELPS PRODUCE THE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH SOME KNOWLEDGE COUNTS AS TRUE, SERIOUS AND AUTHORITATIVE.
For museums:
do not only analyse objects.
Analyse categories, archives, labels, disciplines, institutional authority and the historical struggles hidden behind them.

MICHEL FOUCAULT — “7 JANUARY 1976” (SOCIETY MUST BE DEFENDED)
1. “the insurrection of subjugated knowledges” (Foucault, 2003, p. 7)
USE FOR: genealogy as a recovery/reactivation of knowledges subordinated by dominant systems.
2. “historical contents that have been buried or masked” (Foucault, 2003, p. 7)
USE FOR: the first sense of “subjugated knowledges”.
IMPORTANT: these are exact phrases from the lecture, not paraphrases.

CASTELLS — NETWORK SOCIETY / COMMUNICATION POWER


5. POWER OF THE NETWORK


Castells’ key contribution is that power in contemporary society does not necessarily operate from one visible centre. It increasingly works through networks: through the ability to programme them, connect them, control flows of information, and include or exclude particular nodes.


The important question therefore becomes not only:
Who has power?


But:
Who controls the architecture through which information circulates?
Who defines which nodes connect?
Who can programme the goals of the network?
Who can switch actors or information in and out?


Useful formulation:
“Power is increasingly exercised through the organisation of networks and flows rather than only through direct command.”


This is especially useful for thinking about platforms.
Meta does not need to issue explicit commands to users.
Its power also lies in structuring:
• what becomes visible
• which behaviours are rewarded
• how information circulates
• which connections are amplified
• which signals become meaningful


LINK TO MY ESSAY — NETWORKED SURVEILLANCE


My essay initially frames surveillance through the question:
“Who is watching me?”


Castells helps move beyond the image of a single observer.


There may be no single watcher.


Instead, the subject exists inside interconnected systems in which:
• Meta collects one set of behavioural data
• WHOOP collects physiological data
• Google collects another set of signals
• advertising infrastructures connect and interpret behavioural traces
• algorithms classify, predict and return outputs


Surveillance therefore becomes networked.


Not:
“Big Brother watches you.”


But:
“You continuously generate data across interconnected networks.”


This gives a more contemporary model of power.


The subject is not simply visible to one authority.
They are continuously rendered legible across multiple infrastructures whose data, classifications and feedback loops overlap.


Potential essay use:
Castells can help explain why the classical surveillance model is insufficient for contemporary digital culture.


Foucault helps explain visibility and self-regulation.
Zuboff helps explain behavioural extraction and prediction.
Castells can help explain the distributed infrastructure through which these processes operate.


Strong possible sentence:
“Contemporary surveillance is less a single gaze than a distributed architecture of capture, circulation and interpretation.”


Another:
“The question is no longer only who watches, but how networks make subjects continuously legible across systems.”

14/10 lecture 
trouillot: 
history as 1 action 2 as a narrative 
history has a semantic ambiguity 1 socio historical process 2 our story of that process 


history is always produced in a specific context/ historical actors are also narrators and vice versa (e.g. napoleon) 
Vice versa is a Latin phrase meaning "the other way around" or "with the order turned around"






TROUILLOT — THREE QUICK EXAMPLES OF THE FOUR MOMENTS OF HISTORICAL PRODUCTION


1. USSR / THE HOLODOMOR
Fact creation: many experiences were not formally recorded, and some records were suppressed or destroyed.
Fact assembly: Soviet archives privileged state documentation and restricted access to material that challenged the official account.
Fact retrieval: official Soviet narratives did not recognise the famine as a distinct political catastrophe.
Retrospective significance: after the collapse of the USSR, the Holodomor acquired much greater public, scholarly and political visibility.


2. BENIN BRONZES / BRITISH COLONIAL HISTORY
Fact creation: the 1897 British expedition was extensively documented by military and colonial actors, while Edo perspectives were less systematically preserved in British records.
Fact assembly: military, auction and museum records survived and became the dominant archival base.
Fact retrieval: older museum narratives often foregrounded craftsmanship, collection history or acquisition while backgrounding violent seizure.
Retrospective significance: restitution debates have made the history of looting and colonial violence central to contemporary interpretation.


3. LESS OBVIOUS EXAMPLE — WOMEN’S UNPAID DOMESTIC LABOUR
Fact creation: housework, childcare and care work were rarely documented as “economic production” because they happened inside the household and often generated no wage records.
Fact assembly: state archives, censuses and labour statistics historically privileged paid employment, so domestic labour appeared only indirectly or was categorised as economic inactivity.
Fact retrieval: conventional histories of industrialisation focused on factories, wages and male employment, making unpaid reproductive labour largely invisible.
Retrospective significance: feminist and social historians later reframed domestic labour as essential to the reproduction of the workforce and therefore to the economy itself.


WHY THIS THIRD EXAMPLE IS GOOD
It shows that silence does not always require censorship. A history can become invisible simply because institutions never created categories capable of recording it.


Strong seminar line:
“Trouillot’s model is useful because silence can be produced not only by suppression, but by the categories through which institutions decide what is worth recording in the first place.”


Even shorter:
“Silence can be bureaucratic before it becomes ideological.”




TROUILLOT — MOMENTS OF POWER AND SILENCING
(added from seminar slide)


Four moments of silencing can enter the production of history:


1. SOURCES
Silence can enter before an archive even exists.
Examples:
• sources are not preserved
• evidence never comes to light
• records are destroyed
• people do not share their stories
• people forget or die before testimony is recorded
• false or misleading sources survive instead


Key question:
What was never recorded, preserved or allowed to become evidence?


2. ARCHIVES
Silence can enter through the organisation of evidence.
Questions:
• Who collects the material?
• What is included and what is excluded?
• What is prioritised?
• How is it catalogued and described through metadata?
• Who gets access?
• Who acts as gatekeeper?
• How is material named and framed?


Important:
Archival power is not only about possession. Metadata, naming and access structures can determine how a source becomes intelligible.


3. NARRATIVES
Silence can enter when evidence is turned into a story.
Questions:
• Who gets to tell the story?
• What is included or omitted?
• Who or what is prioritised?
• Who is misrepresented?
• Whose interests does the narrative uphold?


Useful connection:
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Can the Subaltern Speak?”
The key issue is not simply whether marginalised people literally speak, but whether dominant structures allow their speech to become legible, audible and authoritative.


4. RETROSPECTIVE SIGNIFICANCE
Trouillot calls this “history in the final instance”.
Silence enters through later judgments about importance.


Questions:
• Who or what is deemed historically significant?
• Who or what is treated as marginal?
• Which events become commemorated, taught and institutionalised?
• Which remain peripheral despite surviving evidence?


CORE POINT
Power operates at every stage:
SOURCE → ARCHIVE → NARRATIVE → SIGNIFICANCE


So historical silence is cumulative.
An absence in a museum display may have begun decades or centuries earlier, before the curator ever encountered the material.


Strong seminar line:
“Silence is not a single omission at the point of narration; it can be produced cumulatively across the entire historical process.”


Another useful formulation:
“The archive does not simply preserve history. It also preserves earlier acts of selection.”

SEMESTER ESSAY — A-LEVEL PEEL STRUCTURE


WORKING TITLE
Behaviour as Material: Datafication, Self-Surveillance and Power in Digital Art


CENTRAL RESEARCH QUESTION
Why do contemporary subjects voluntarily submit themselves to continuous measurement, and what forms of power emerge when surveillance is experienced as self-knowledge rather than coercion?


CORE THESIS
Contemporary digital power does not operate only by watching us; it works by translating behaviour into measurable, interpretable and actionable data. We do not necessarily desire surveillance itself. We desire certainty, optimisation and self-knowledge — and surveillance increasingly arrives disguised as all three.


KEY LINE TO KEEP
“The contemporary subject is not merely watched; it learns to want a measurable version of itself.”


A-LEVEL STRATEGY
This essay must NOT become:
• a survey of digital surveillance
• a list of theorists
• a list of digital artworks
• an argument that “technology is bad”


It needs to make one precise claim and test it through a small number of cases.


The strongest argumentative progression is:
BEHAVIOUR → DATA → CLASSIFICATION → FEEDBACK → SELF-REGULATION


The essay should move from external measurement to voluntary self-measurement, then return to art to ask whether digital artworks can expose or interrupt that process.


WORD BUDGET — APPROX. 2,500 WORDS
Introduction: 250–300
PEEL 1: 400–450
PEEL 2: 500–550
PEEL 3: 550–600
PEEL 4: 400–450
Conclusion: 200–250


MAIN THEORY ONLY
Michel Foucault
Shoshana Zuboff
Lev Manovich


Secondary / contextual support only:
Tony Bennett
one neoliberalism reading from the unit
optional: Deleuze if genuinely needed


Do not introduce more theorists unless they solve a specific problem.


MAIN ART CASES
1. Angeli — Fashion Police, Peckham Digital
2. ONE second major case: ideally Rafael Lozano-Hemmer OR Lauren Lee McCarthy


COUNTER-CASE / FINAL CRITICAL TURN
Hito Steyerl OR Lauren Lee McCarthy, depending on which artist is not used as the second major case.


The essay should analyse a maximum of 2 major artworks + 1 short counter-case.


INTRODUCTION — 250–300 WORDS


OPENING
Begin with the encounter at Peckham Digital.


Describe the moment rather than immediately theorising it:
you participated in Fashion Police and became aware that your appearance / behaviour was not simply being seen by another person but translated through a technical system.


Questions generated by the encounter:
What exactly is being tracked?
What counts as meaningful information?
How does a system turn behaviour into a category?
Who decides what the category means?


Then introduce your situated professional perspective:
working in performance marketing has made behavioural translation familiar.


Human actions routinely appear as:
clicks
views
leads
purchases
conversions
audiences
events


Meta Ads and GA4 are useful here as PRIMARY OPERATIONAL EVIDENCE, not as theory.


Strong possible sentence:
“Working in performance marketing has made the translation of behaviour into events familiar to me; encountering Fashion Police made that familiar technical process appear politically strange.”


Then introduce self-tracking:
WHOOP makes bodily states legible as metrics such as sleep, recovery, strain, heart rate and HRV.


This produces the deeper question:
why do people willingly seek more measurement?


Avoid claiming:
“humans naturally want metrics.”


Instead argue:
self-tracking systems frame measurement through promises of certainty, optimisation, care and self-knowledge.


CENTRAL QUESTION
Why do contemporary subjects voluntarily submit themselves to continuous measurement, and what forms of power emerge when surveillance is experienced as self-knowledge rather than coercion?


THESIS
“This essay argues that the key issue is not surveillance as watching, but measurement as a form of power.”


Add:
Measurement becomes politically significant when behaviour is translated into categories, returned to the subject as interpretation, and used to shape future conduct.


PEEL 1 — TO MEASURE IS ALREADY TO INTERPRET
Approx. 400–450 words


P — POINT
Data does not simply record behaviour. Before behaviour can become data, a system must decide what counts as a meaningful event.


E — EVIDENCE
Use:
Google Analytics 4
Meta Ads / Meta Pixel


Examples:
looking at a page → page_view / ViewContent
scrolling → scroll
watching a video → video engagement
buying → Purchase
adding an item → AddToCart


Theory:
Lev Manovich — numerical representation / data structures.


Use Manovich to establish that digital representation depends on selection, coding and formalisation.


E — EXPLANATION
This is the first original claim of the essay:


“Before behaviour can be governed, it must first be made legible.”


The system does not capture a complete person.
It produces a computational model by selecting particular variables.


Strong sentence:
“The data subject is not the person; it is a model of the person produced through selected variables.”


Critical move:
Measurement is therefore not neutral observation.
It already contains:
selection
classification
thresholds
interpretation


Use your performance-marketing experience as situated knowledge:
technical vocabulary such as “events,” “signals,” “audiences,” “conversions” and “optimisation” presents behavioural capture as operational and neutral.


Ask:
What political assumptions disappear when behaviour is described only as a signal?


L — LINK
This logic becomes especially visible in interactive art, where the viewer can literally become the input from which the work operates.


Transition:
“The same operational grammar — capture, classify, respond — structures both advertising infrastructure and many interactive artworks.”


PEEL 2 — THE VIEWER BECOMES MATERIAL
Approx. 500–550 words


P — POINT
Interactive digital art can collapse the distinction between spectator and material: the viewer does not simply interpret the work but generates the data through which the work takes form.


E — EVIDENCE
MAIN CLOSE READING:
Angeli — Fashion Police, Peckham Digital.


Do not summarise the work generally.
Describe:
• what the viewer does
• what the system senses
• what the system appears to infer
• what categories / judgements are produced
• how the viewer experiences being classified
• whether awareness changes behaviour


SECOND ART CASE:
Choose one:
Rafael Lozano-Hemmer — Pulse Index / Zoom Pavilion
OR
Lauren Lee McCarthy — LAUREN / SOMEONE


Tony Bennett can support the shift from spectator to spectacle.
Foucault can support visibility / self-regulation.


E — EXPLANATION
Main argument:
Participation is not automatically agency.


Interactive art is often described as participatory, open or democratic.
But the system still determines:
what can count as input
which actions are legible
how data is interpreted
which outputs are possible


Strong lines:
“Participation is structured freedom.”
“The viewer may be active without being sovereign.”


This is where the essay must distinguish:
activity ≠ control
participation ≠ authorship
visibility ≠ agency


Critical question:
When an artwork asks the viewer to participate, does it redistribute power or simply enrol the viewer more deeply into the system?


L — LINK
Once participation becomes legible and useful to a system, the problem shifts from observation to extraction and prediction.


PEEL 3 — FROM BEING WATCHED TO WANTING TO BE MEASURED
Approx. 550–600 words
THIS IS THE INTELLECTUAL CLIMAX.


P — POINT
The most consequential form of contemporary surveillance may not be imposed observation but voluntary self-measurement.


E — EVIDENCE
WHOOP as the central everyday case.


Possible metrics:
sleep
recovery
strain
heart rate
HRV


Use official WHOOP documentation only to establish what the device measures and how scores are framed.


Theory:
Foucault — technologies of the self
Foucault — governmentality
Foucault — The Birth of Biopolitics / homo oeconomicus as entrepreneur of the self
Unit reading on neoliberalism


Bring in Zuboff here:
The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
especially Chapter 3, “The Discovery of Behavioral Surplus”


Zuboff is useful for:
behavioural data as extractable resource
prediction
commercialisation of behavioural traces


E — EXPLANATION
This section needs explicit THEORETICAL CRITIQUE.


Do not write:
Foucault says X.
Zuboff says Y.
WHOOP does Z.


Instead:


Foucault helps explain why subjects begin to regulate themselves.


Zuboff helps explain how behavioural data becomes economically valuable.


BUT:
neither framework alone fully explains the attraction of self-measurement as pleasure, reassurance, care or self-knowledge.


That gap is where your argument enters.


Core claim:
“We do not necessarily desire surveillance; we desire certainty, optimisation and self-knowledge — and surveillance arrives disguised as all three.”


Another:
“The quantified self does not experience measurement only as surveillance; it can experience it as care, feedback and self-improvement.”


Important nuance:
Do not universalise this psychologically.
Say that self-tracking platforms PRESENT and FRAME measurement through these promises.


Then analyse feedback:
body → sensor → metric → score → recommendation → changed behaviour


Strong claim:
“Measurement becomes governance when interpretation returns to the subject as a norm against which future behaviour is adjusted.”


This is where neoliberal subjectivity becomes important:
the subject is encouraged to monitor, optimise, compare and improve itself.


Possible critical sentence:
“Neoliberal power becomes especially effective when optimisation is experienced as personal freedom.”


L — LINK
The Big Brother model is therefore insufficient.
Contemporary power does not always need to force observation from outside; subjects may actively seek the systems through which they become measurable.


PEEL 4 — CAN DIGITAL ART INTERRUPT THE FEEDBACK LOOP?
Approx. 400–450 words


P — POINT
Digital art can make measurement perceptible, but simply reproducing surveillance technologies does not automatically make an artwork critical.


E — EVIDENCE
Use ONE counter-case:
Hito Steyerl — How Not to Be Seen
OR
Lauren Lee McCarthy if not already used.


Return briefly to Fashion Police.


Possible concepts:
illegibility
refusal
misclassification
opacity
counter-surveillance


E — EXPLANATION
Main critical distinction:
Visibility is not the same as critique.


An artwork can:
reveal surveillance
but also aestheticise surveillance.


Therefore the critical question is not simply:
Does the work show tracking?


Ask:
Does it reveal who defines the categories?
Does it expose asymmetry?
Does it permit refusal?
Does it destabilise the meaning assigned to data?
Does it make space for what cannot be measured?


Strong question:
“What should remain unmeasured?”


This is the most important return to art:
digital art becomes politically significant when it makes the apparently neutral process of measurement strange, visible and contestable.


L — LINK
The politics of measurement is therefore the politics of deciding what can be made legible, by whom, and toward what ends.


CONCLUSION — 200–250 WORDS


Do not summarise each paragraph mechanically.


Answer the research question directly.


THREE FINDINGS


1. MEASUREMENT IS NOT NEUTRAL
Behaviour does not naturally arrive as data.
Systems produce data through selection, classification and interpretation.


2. PARTICIPATION IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY AGENCY
Interactive systems can make viewers active while still determining the terms through which that activity becomes meaningful.


3. SURVEILLANCE IS NOT ALWAYS EXPERIENCED AS COERCION
Self-tracking shows how measurement can be welcomed when it appears as care, certainty, optimisation or self-knowledge.


MAIN SHIFT
The essay moves from:
surveillance as observation


to:
measurement as continuous behavioural governance.


Strong conclusion:
“Digital art becomes politically significant when it interrupts the apparent neutrality of this process and makes visible not only that we are measured, but how measurement produces particular versions of who we are.”


FINAL SENTENCE — KEEP
“The question is no longer simply who is watching us, but who gets to decide what about us is measurable, what those measurements mean, and how they will be used to shape what we do next.”


WHAT MAKES THIS A-LEVEL RATHER THAN B-LEVEL


B-LEVEL VERSION:
Foucault says this.
Zuboff says this.
WHOOP does this.
Fashion Police shows surveillance.


A-LEVEL VERSION:
Foucault explains self-regulation but his disciplinary model becomes less sufficient when subjects actively purchase and desire measurement.
Zuboff explains extraction and prediction but does not fully explain the pleasure and reassurance of being quantified.
The artwork becomes a site where these tensions can be tested rather than merely illustrated.


Every major paragraph should contain:
1. a claim
2. evidence
3. close analysis
4. a limitation / tension / alternative interpretation
5. a link back to the research question


UAL LEVEL 5 — A CHECKLIST


ENQUIRY
Show a clear line of inquiry from Peckham Digital to the final research question.
Demonstrate that the question developed through research rather than arriving fully formed.
Use diverse sources but only where they advance the inquiry.


KNOWLEDGE
Do not demonstrate knowledge by adding more theorists.
Demonstrate it by showing where theories agree, conflict or become insufficient.


PROCESS
Keep evidence of:
initial Big Tech patronage idea
narrowing after tutor feedback
Peckham Digital encounter
movement toward behaviour / measurement
selection and rejection of case studies


This development itself is evidence of critical research process.


COMMUNICATION
One argument per section.
Define specialist terms the first time they appear.
Avoid dense theory-dumping.
Use first person only when it adds methodological value.


REALISATION
The final essay should feel deliberately edited.
Two major art cases are stronger than six shallow ones.
Every example must earn its place.


READING YOU SHOULD DO YOURSELF


SHOSHANA ZUBOFF
The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
Essential:
Chapter 3 — “The Discovery of Behavioral Surplus”
Then selectively read sections on prediction and behavioural modification.


Read with three questions:
1. What transforms behaviour into an economic resource?
2. Where does Zuboff position the user as relatively passive?
3. Can her framework explain why self-measurement feels useful or pleasurable?


MICHEL FOUCAULT
Discipline and Punish — “Panopticism”
Technologies of the Self
The Birth of Biopolitics — especially neoliberalism / entrepreneur of the self


Read with:
What changes when discipline is no longer visibly imposed from outside?


LEV MANOVICH
The Language of New Media
Focus:
Numerical Representation
Automation
Variability
Database / interface where useful


Read with:
What has to happen before lived behaviour becomes computational data?


PRIMARY TECH SOURCES
Google Analytics 4 official documentation
Meta official event / Pixel documentation
WHOOP official documentation


Use these as evidence of operational language, not neutral theoretical authority.


FINAL RESEARCH PRINCIPLE
The essay should not prove that surveillance exists.


It should prove something more specific:


Contemporary systems gain power by translating behaviour into measurable categories and returning those measurements to subjects as apparently useful knowledge about themselves.


Digital art matters because it can expose the construction, interpretation and political consequences of that process.

SEMESTER PROJECT CONCEPT — ESSAY + WEBSITE


WORKING ESSAY TITLE
Behaviour as Material: Participation, Data and Power in Digital Art


ORIGIN OF THE PROJECT
The project developed directly from visiting Peckham Digital and seeing Angeli’s Fashion Police. The work triggered a set of very immediate questions:
• What can be tracked?
• How is behaviour translated into data?
• What becomes measurable?
• Who decides which behaviours are meaningful?
• When does participation become extraction?
• What happens when the viewer is no longer simply looking at an artwork, but actively producing the material it runs on?


This became the conceptual starting point for thinking about digital art not simply as art made with technology, but as a field in which human behaviour itself can become a medium.


CENTRAL RESEARCH QUESTION
How does contemporary digital art turn human behaviour into material, and what does this reveal about datafication, surveillance and contemporary forms of power?


SECONDARY QUESTIONS
1. What happens when behaviour — movement, clicks, biometric information, attention, participation — becomes the input of an artwork?
2. Where is the boundary between participation and extraction?
3. How do interactive artworks reproduce, expose or interrupt the same logics through which digital platforms measure, predict and monetise everyday behaviour?
4. What kinds of power emerge when subjects voluntarily produce themselves as data?
5. What can and cannot be measured, and what gets lost when human behaviour is translated into metrics?


WORKING THESIS
In contemporary digital culture, behaviour is no longer merely observed; it is continuously captured, quantified, predicted and fed back into systems. Interactive digital art can make this condition perceptible by turning the viewer’s behaviour into the material of the work itself. These artworks therefore offer a way to examine the unstable boundary between agency and extraction, participation and surveillance, self-expression and self-measurement.


A possible core formulation:
“The artwork and the platform may share an operational grammar — capture, process, respond — while producing radically different relations of power.”


WHY “BEHAVIOUR AS MATERIAL”
Traditional artistic media:
paint
stone
film
photography


Digital / interactive media can also work with:
movement
attention
voice
touch
heartbeat
facial expression
location
clicks
time spent
social interaction
biometric signals
behavioural patterns


The important conceptual shift is:
the viewer is not only interpreting the work.
The viewer may also become an input into the work.


This raises a political question:
If behaviour can become artistic material, it can also become economic material.


This is where digital art connects to the wider data economy.


THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK


1. MICHEL FOUCAULT — POWER, SURVEILLANCE, GOVERNMENTALITY
Useful concepts:
• surveillance
• discipline
• normalisation
• self-regulation
• power as relational rather than simply possessed
• governmentality
• technologies of the self


Key shift:
power does not only prohibit.
It produces subjects who learn to regulate themselves.


This becomes particularly useful for digital culture because much contemporary monitoring is voluntary:
we track ourselves
measure ourselves
optimise ourselves
publish ourselves
compare ourselves


Strong question:
What happens when surveillance becomes self-surveillance?


2. SHOSHANA ZUBOFF — SURVEILLANCE CAPITALISM
Key concept:
behaviour becomes raw material.


Digital platforms extract behavioural data and use it to:
• analyse
• predict
• influence
• modify future behaviour


This gives the essay its political-economic dimension.


Important distinction:
Foucault helps explain the form of power.
Zuboff helps explain the economic infrastructure in which behavioural data acquires value.


3. LEV MANOVICH — DIGITAL MEDIA / INTERFACE / DATABASE
Useful for understanding why digital artworks can behave as systems rather than fixed objects.


Key ideas:
• programmability
• variability
• modularity
• database logic
• interface
• interactivity


Question:
If an artwork changes according to user input, where is the artwork located?
In the code?
The interface?
The participant?
The feedback loop?


Possible argument:
Interactive digital art redistributes authorship between artist, software and user — but that freedom is always structured by the system.


Strong formulation:
“Participation is structured freedom.”


4. NEOLIBERALISM
The neoliberal subject is encouraged to continuously:
• monitor itself
• optimise itself
• compete
• measure performance
• turn identity into a project
• understand success through metrics


Examples from ordinary life:
WHOOP
Apple Watch
Fitbit
Oura Ring
Strava
sleep scores
readiness scores
productivity apps
screen-time metrics
social media engagement
likes
followers
conversion rates
personal branding analytics


These devices are important because they make the logic of datafication intimate and voluntary.


The subject does not merely tolerate measurement.
The subject often wants more measurement.


Strong question:
Why do we experience quantified self-surveillance as empowerment?


5. TONY BENNETT — THE EXHIBITIONARY COMPLEX
Useful for the viewer as simultaneously observer and observed.


The museum/exhibition is not only a place of looking.
It organises:
• visibility
• conduct
• spectatorship
• self-regulation


Connection to interactive digital art:
the viewer can become part of the display and part of the data produced by the display.


6. POSSIBLE DELEUZE ADDITION — SOCIETIES OF CONTROL
Useful bridge between Foucault’s enclosed disciplinary institutions and contemporary networked forms of tracking.


Instead of:
school / prison / factory as discrete enclosures


digital control can become:
continuous
distributed
adaptive
networked


This could help explain why “Big Brother” today does not necessarily look like a central watcher.


It can exist as infrastructure.


KEY CONCEPTUAL MOVE
Do not make the essay simply:
“surveillance is everywhere.”


Instead:
analyse the form of power produced through measurement.


The important question is not only:
Who is watching?


But:
Who is measuring?
What becomes measurable?
How is behaviour translated into data?
What actions become predictable?
What forms of subjectivity emerge when people learn to understand themselves through metrics?


CASE STUDY STRATEGY
Use a small number of artworks — ideally 2–3.


The argument should emerge from the works rather than forcing a huge survey of digital art.


POSSIBLE CASES


1. ANGELI — FASHION POLICE, PECKHAM DIGITAL
Conceptual starting point.


Use it to establish:
• tracking
• computational interpretation of appearance / behaviour
• categorisation
• visibility
• the politics of machine-readable identity


Possible opening:
The essay begins with the experience of encountering Fashion Police at Peckham Digital and realising that the interesting question was not simply whether digital systems watch us, but what they are capable of recognising, classifying and measuring.


2. LAUREN LEE MCCARTHY
Especially useful for:
• automated intimacy
• algorithmic social relations
• domestic surveillance
• participation
• human behaviour mediated by systems


Her work allows the essay to move from surveillance as observation to surveillance as social relationship.


3. RAFAEL LOZANO-HEMMER — PULSE INDEX
Fingerprint + heartbeat become part of a database and visual installation.


Strong because:
body → biometric signal → data → image → archive


The work literalises the transformation of the individual into measurable information.


4. RAFAEL LOZANO-HEMMER — ZOOM PAVILION
The viewer enters the space and becomes tracked through surveillance systems.


Useful for:
Foucault
Bennett
viewer as observer / observed
machine vision


5. HITO STEYERL — HOW NOT TO BE SEEN
A useful counterpoint:
instead of asking how to participate, asks how to become illegible or invisible.


This introduces the politics of refusal.


If contemporary systems demand visibility and legibility:
can disappearance become a form of resistance?


6. TREVOR PAGLEN / KATE CRAWFORD
Useful for:
machine vision
classification
training datasets
how humans become categories within computational systems


Possible use:
to move from behavioural capture to the politics of classification.


EVERYDAY TECHNOLOGY AS A PARALLEL CASE
The essay can use consumer tracking technologies briefly as cultural context rather than full case studies.


WHOOP / OURA / APPLE WATCH / FITBIT:
The body is continuously translated into:
heart rate
sleep
stress
recovery
steps
readiness
performance


This creates a useful conceptual parallel with interactive art.


The same basic operation:
BODY / BEHAVIOUR → SENSOR → DATA → INTERPRETATION → FEEDBACK


But the political purpose differs.


This is one of the essay’s most interesting tensions:
An artwork and a commercial platform may use similar technical processes while producing very different meanings and relations of power.


POSSIBLE ESSAY STRUCTURE


INTRODUCTION
Start with Fashion Police at Peckham Digital.


Personal observation:
The work produced a very immediate realisation that contemporary digital culture does not simply represent us — it measures us.


Introduce questions:
What can be measured?
Who defines the categories?
What happens when human behaviour becomes machine-readable?


Introduce thesis.


SECTION 1 — FROM SURVEILLANCE TO DATAFICATION
Foucault → discipline / visibility / self-regulation
Zuboff → behavioural data / extraction / prediction


Key transition:
Contemporary surveillance increasingly moves from watching behaviour to operationalising behaviour.


SECTION 2 — BEHAVIOUR AS ARTISTIC MATERIAL
Manovich → interactive digital systems
Case studies: Fashion Police + Lozano-Hemmer / McCarthy


Analyse exactly how each work captures and transforms viewer input.


Question:
Is the participant exercising agency or entering a prestructured feedback system?


SECTION 3 — THE MEASURED SELF
Neoliberalism + Foucault’s governmentality.


Bring in WHOOP, Oura, Apple Watch etc.


Argument:
Measurement becomes internalised as self-care, productivity and optimisation.


This complicates the Big Brother metaphor:
the contemporary subject often participates willingly in its own measurement.


Strong formulation:
“Big Brother no longer needs to watch continuously from above when the subject has learned to monitor itself.”


SECTION 4 — PARTICIPATION OR EXTRACTION?
Compare artistic and commercial systems.


Ask:
When is capturing user behaviour critical?
When is it extractive?
Can an artwork reproduce surveillance technologies without normalising them?


Possibly introduce Steyerl / refusal / illegibility.


CONCLUSION
Digital art is useful not simply because it depicts surveillance, but because it can stage the mechanisms through which behaviour becomes data.


Its critical potential lies in making the infrastructure of measurement perceptible.


The question is therefore not simply whether we are watched.
It is what kinds of subjects we become when measurement is embedded in everyday life.


WEBSITE CONCEPT


WORKING IDEA
The website should not merely illustrate the essay.
It should perform the essay’s argument.


The visitor enters a seemingly simple digital environment and gradually becomes aware of how much information their interaction produces.


Possible central concept:
WHAT CAN BE MEASURED?


The site could progressively reveal that ordinary actions can become data.


Possible interactions:
• cursor movement
• scroll speed
• time spent on page
• click frequency
• hesitation before clicking
• screen size
• device type
• approximate location only if ethically and technically appropriate
• interaction patterns
• choices between images
• response time
• typing rhythm if the user actively enters text


IMPORTANT:
The website should not secretly collect or store personal information.
The conceptual point can be demonstrated transparently, locally and ethically.


A strong structure could be:


PAGE 1 — YOU ARE LOOKING
Minimal screen.
The visitor assumes they are simply observing.


PAGE 2 — THE SYSTEM IS ALSO LOOKING
The site begins showing interaction metrics:
“You have been here for 18 seconds.”
“You moved your cursor X times.”
“You paused here.”
“You scrolled faster here.”


PAGE 3 — YOU BECOME DATA
The metrics become visual material:
graphs
traces
heat-map-like movement
behavioural profile
abstract data portrait


PAGE 4 — INTERPRETATION
The website begins making deliberately questionable interpretations:
“restless”
“decisive”
“hesitant”
“engaged”


This is where the politics becomes visible:
data does not simply record behaviour.
Systems interpret behaviour.


PAGE 5 — WHO DECIDES WHAT THIS MEANS?
Expose the categories.


Connect to:
Foucault
Zuboff
Manovich
neoliberal self-measurement


PAGE 6 — REFUSAL / ILLEGIBILITY
Give the visitor the option to:
erase
obscure
randomise
refuse measurement


Possible Steyerl connection:
What would it mean not to be seen — or not to be legible?


WEBSITE THESIS
The site moves the visitor through three positions:


OBSERVER → DATA SUBJECT → CRITICAL OBSERVER


This mirrors the essay’s argument.


Possible title:
Behaviour as Material


Other possibilities:
The Measured Viewer
You Are the Input
What Can Be Measured?
Terms of Participation
Readiness Score
User Behaviour
Measured / Misread


STRONG OVERALL PROJECT FORMULA
ESSAY:
How does behaviour become data, and what forms of power operate through its measurement?


WEBSITE:
What does it feel like to realise that your behaviour is already producing data?


Together:
the essay theorises measurement.
the website stages it.


LONGER-TERM CONNECTION
This project can remain narrow enough for a 2,500-word essay while later feeding into the larger dissertation-scale interest in Big Tech, cultural infrastructure, sponsorship and the politics of digital art.


The current essay therefore becomes a focused study of one mechanism:
BEHAVIOURAL DATA AS A FORM OF POWER.

CASTELLS — NETWORK SOCIETY / COMMUNICATION POWER


5. POWER OF THE NETWORK


Castells’ key contribution is that power in contemporary society does not necessarily operate from one visible centre. It increasingly works through networks: through the ability to programme them, connect them, control flows of information, and include or exclude particular nodes.


The important question therefore becomes not only:
Who has power?


But:
Who controls the architecture through which information circulates?
Who defines which nodes connect?
Who can programme the goals of the network?
Who can switch actors or information in and out?


Useful formulation:
“Power is increasingly exercised through the organisation of networks and flows rather than only through direct command.”


This is especially useful for thinking about platforms.
Meta does not need to issue explicit commands to users.
Its power also lies in structuring:
• what becomes visible
• which behaviours are rewarded
• how information circulates
• which connections are amplified
• which signals become meaningful


LINK TO MY ESSAY — NETWORKED SURVEILLANCE


My essay initially frames surveillance through the question:
“Who is watching me?”


Castells helps move beyond the image of a single observer.


There may be no single watcher.


Instead, the subject exists inside interconnected systems in which:
• Meta collects one set of behavioural data
• WHOOP collects physiological data
• Google collects another set of signals
• advertising infrastructures connect and interpret behavioural traces
• algorithms classify, predict and return outputs


Surveillance therefore becomes networked.


Not:
“Big Brother watches you.”


But:
“You continuously generate data across interconnected networks.”


This gives a more contemporary model of power.


The subject is not simply visible to one authority.
They are continuously rendered legible across multiple infrastructures whose data, classifications and feedback loops overlap.


Potential essay use:
Castells can help explain why the classical surveillance model is insufficient for contemporary digital culture.


Foucault helps explain visibility and self-regulation.
Zuboff helps explain behavioural extraction and prediction.
Castells can help explain the distributed infrastructure through which these processes operate.


Strong possible sentence:
“Contemporary surveillance is less a single gaze than a distributed architecture of capture, circulation and interpretation.”


Another:
“The question is no longer only who watches, but how networks make subjects continuously legible across systems.”

This will make the site feel like a curatorial argument rather than a database.

• the historical development of surveillance and participatory digital art

• how digital art entered biennials, festivals and major institutions

1. EXHIBITION ARTISTS

2. RESEARCH LINEAGE

it demonstrates historical and institutional awareness without pretending that museum-scale artists are realistically available for an emerging exhibition.


F. STRONG CURATORIAL FORMULATION
